en.note:
The idea

Besides the voltooide tijd (unit 19), Dutch has a one-word past tense: the verleden tijd. Ik werkte can mean "I worked", "I was working" or "I used to work", depending on the context. It looks like the English simple past, but it's used a bit differently: in conversation Dutch prefers the perfect to say what happened, and keeps the simple past mainly for descriptions, habits and stories.

Weak verbs: -te(n) or -de(n)

You add -te (plural -ten) or -de (plural -den) to the stem, a bit like English -ed. The choice follows the same rule as the participle: 't kofschip. If the stem ends in t, k, f, s, ch, p → -te; otherwise → -de. There is one form for the whole singular.

werkenwonenreizen
ik / jij / hijwerktewoondereisde
wij / jullie / zijwerktenwoondenreisden

As with the participle, look at the infinitive: reizen has a z → reisde. If the stem already ends in t or d, you write two consonants even though you hear only one: wachten → wachtte.

Strong and irregular verbs: the vowel changes

Strong verbs take no ending in the singular: they change their vowel, just like English drink → drank or come → came. In the plural they add -en. They're the most common verbs, so they're worth learning right away (notice how many look like their English cousins):

infinitivesingularplural
zijnwaswaren
hebbenhadhadden
gaanginggingen
komenkwamkwamen
zienzagzagen
etenataten
lezenlaslazen
drinkendronkdronken

Modal verbs have their own forms too: kunnen → kon, moeten → moest, mogen → mocht, willen → wilde (or wou). And kopen → kocht.

In separable verbs the particle goes to the end, as in the present: We kwamen om acht uur aan.

When to use it: verleden tijd or voltooide tijd?

  • Voltooide tijd (ik heb gewerkt): to say what happened, especially in conversation, even where English uses the simple past. Wat heb je gisteren gedaan? — Ik heb een film gezien. (What did you do yesterday? — I saw a movie.)
  • Verleden tijd (ik werkte): to describe a situation or a habit in the past, like English "was ...ing" or "used to". Vroeger woonde ik in een klein dorp. Het regende. It's also used to tell a series of events, in stories and books.
  • With zijn, hebben and the modals the verleden tijd is completely normal in speech too: Ik was moe, We hadden honger, Ik moest werken.

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Treating a strong verb as weak: ik gade, ik komde → ik ging, ik kwam.
  • Mixing up -te/-de: woonte → woonde, werkde → werkte.
  • Forgetting the plural, since English "was" has no plural ending: wij was → wij waren.
  • Using the simple past for every past event as in English: in conversation Ik heb gisteren een film gezien sounds more natural than Ik zag gisteren een film.
  • Looking for an "-ing" form: "I was reading" is simply ik las.
en.vlaams: For "I wanted" in speech you often hear ik wou instead of ik wilde, in Belgium as well as in the Netherlands: both forms are correct. With gij/ge the past of zijn is waart: "Waart ge moe?" (were you tired?).

hard.e: After Vroeger there's inversion, but the subject is mijn opa (singular): kwam. Komen is strong, so no -de (like English come → came).

g.kwamen: plural: the subject mijn opa is singular

hard.tt: My grandpa used to come to our village by bus every Sunday.

hard.q: Vorige zomer ___ we drie weken in Oostende en het ___ bijna elke dag.
hard.e: we is plural → waren; het is singular → regende (n isn't in kofschip: -de).

g.zijn … regent: present: the sentence is about last summer

hard.tt: Last summer we spent three weeks in Ostend and it rained almost every day.

hard.e: Stem wacht + -te (t is in kofschip): you write two t's, wachtte, even though you hear only one.
hard.tt: My brother used to wait half an hour for the tram every morning.

hard.e: Modal in the past, plural: kunnen → konden; the infinitive komen stays at the end.
hard.tt: We couldn't come yesterday, because our car had broken down.
